text: Article 55 § 3 of the Russian Constitution provides that the rights and freedoms of individuals and citizens may be limited by federal law only to the extent required for the protection of the fundamental principles of the constitutional system, morality, health, the rights and lawful interests of other people, and for ensuring the defence of the country and the security of the State.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: The Federal Law on Gatherings, Meetings, Demonstrations, Processions and Pickets, no. 54-FZ of 19 June 2004 (the Public Events Act), Section 2, defines a public event as an open, peaceful action accessible to all, held in the form of a gathering, a meeting, a demonstration, a march, or a picket or in various combinations of these forms, organised at the initiative of citizens of the Russian Federation, political parties, other public associations, or religious associations, including events held with the use of vehicles.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: The Public Events Act, Section 2, provides that the aim of a public event is the free expression and formation of opinions, and to put forward demands on issues of political, economic, social and cultural life in the country, as well as issues of foreign policy.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: The Public Events Act, Section 3, provides that a public event is based on the principle of legality, meaning compliance with the provisions of the Russian Constitution, the Public Events Act, and other legislative acts of the Russian Federation.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: The Public Events Act, Section 5 § 4, provides that the organiser of a public event must notify the executive or municipal authority of the public event in accordance with Section 7 of the Public Events Act.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: The Public Events Act, Section 7, provides that notification of a public event (except for a gathering and a picket held by a solo participant) must be filed in writing by its organiser with the executive or municipal authority no earlier than fifteen days and no later than ten days before the date of the public event.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: The Public Events Act, Section 16, provides that the grounds for ending a public event include: the emergence of a genuine threat to citizens' lives or health, and to the possessions of physical or legal persons; commission by the participants of unlawful acts or a deliberate breach by the organiser of the requirements on the procedure for the conduct of public events; and (following legislative amendments of 8 June 2012) non-compliance by the organisers with the obligations set out in Section 5 § 4 of the Public Events Act.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: The Public Events Act, Section 17 § 1, provides that if it is decided to end the public event, the representative of the executive or municipal authority shall give an order to the organiser to end the public event, having explained the reasons for its termination, and within twenty-four hours shall issue this order in writing and serve it on the organiser; shall set the time for compliance with the order; and if the organiser does not comply, shall directly address the participants and set an additional time for compliance.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: The Public Events Act, Section 17 § 2, provides that in the event of non-compliance with the order to end the public event, the police shall take the necessary measures to end the public event.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: The Public Events Act, Section 17 § 3, provides that the procedure for ending a public event set out in Section 17 § 1 shall not apply in the event of mass disorder, mob violence, arson, or other situations requiring urgent action.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: The Public Events Act, Section 17 § 4, provides that failure to obey lawful orders from police officers or resistance to them by certain participants of the public event may incur liability as provided for by law.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: The Public Events Act, Section 18 § 1, provides that the organiser of a public event, officials and other citizens shall not be entitled to prevent the participants in a public event from expressing their opinions in a manner that does not violate public order and the procedure for holding a public event.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Prior to 8 June 2012, Article 19 § 3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provided that failure to obey a lawful order or demand of a police officer in connection with the performance of their official duties related to maintaining public order and security, or impeding the performance by them of their official duties, shall be punishable by a fine of between RUB 500 and RUB 1,000 or by administrative imprisonment of up to fifteen days.
section_path: THE FACTS

text: Prior to 8 June 2012, Article 20 § 2 (1) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provided that breaches of the established procedure for the organisation of public gatherings, meetings, demonstrations, marches or pickets shall be punishable by an administrative fine of between ten and twenty times the minimum wage, payable by the organisers.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Prior to 8 June 2012, Article 20 § 2 (2) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provided that breaches of the established procedure for the conduct of public gatherings, meetings, demonstrations, marches or pickets shall be punishable by an administrative fine of between RUB 1,000 and RUB 2,000 for the organisers, and between RUB 500 and RUB 1,000 for the participants.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Article 27 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that the transfer of an individual to a police station for the purpose of drawing up an administrative offence report, if this cannot be done at the place where the offence was discovered and if the drawing up of a report is mandatory, shall be carried out by the police, and the transfer operation shall be carried out as quickly as possible.
section_path: THE FACTS

text: Article 27 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that the transfer shall be recorded in a transfer operation report, an administrative offence report or an administrative detention report, and the transferred person shall be given a copy of the transfer operation report if he or she so requests.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Article 27 § 3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that administrative detention or short-term restriction of an individual's liberty may be applied in exceptional cases if this is necessary for the prompt and proper examination of the alleged administrative offence or to secure the enforcement of any penalty imposed by a judgment concerning an administrative offence.
section_path: THE FACTS

text: Article 27 § 3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that where the detained person so requests, his or her family, the administrative department at his or her place of work or study and his or her defence counsel shall be informed of his or her whereabouts.
section_path: THE FACTS

text: Article 27 § 3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that the detained person shall have his or her rights and obligations under the Code explained to him or her, and the corresponding entry shall be made in the administrative arrest report.
section_path: THE FACTS

text: Following the amendments of 8 June 2012 (Law no. 65-FZ), a breach of the procedure for organising or running a public event by an organiser became punishable by a fine of between RUB 10,000 and RUB 20,000 or up to forty hours of community work under Article 20 § 2 (1) of the Code of Administrative Offences.

text: The Supreme Court Resolution of 26 June 2018 indicated that an organiser's failure to notify a public event was to be classified under Article 20 § 2 (2-4) of the Code of Administrative Offences, whereas the holding of a public event which had been refused by the authorities constituted an offence on the part of the organiser under Article 20 § 2 (1) of the Code (§§ 28-29 of the Supreme Court Resolution).

IV, 1977, pp. 130, 179-181 and 955) states that the international collective guarantee has as its purpose to ensure that no State shall aim at suppressing the guaranteed freedom by means of minor measures which, while made with the pretext of organising the exercise of freedoms or safeguarding the letter of the law, have the opposite effect.

IV. PREPARATORY WORKS

text: The preparatory work on Article 18 of the Convention states that it is legitimate and necessary to limit, sometimes even to restrain, individual freedoms to allow everyone the peaceful exercise of their freedom and to ensure the maintenance of morality, of the general well-being, of the common good and of public need.
section_path: THE FACTS
IV. PREPARATORY WORKS

text: The preparatory work on Article 18 of the Convention states that when the State defines, organises, regulates and limits freedoms in the interest of the general well-being, it is only fulfilling its duty and such action is permissible and legitimate.
section_path: THE FACTS
IV. PREPARATORY WORKS

text: The preparatory work on Article 18 of the Convention states that when the State intervenes to suppress, restrain and limit freedoms for reasons of state, to protect itself against an opposition it considers dangerous, or to destroy fundamental freedoms it ought to guarantee, then it acts against public interest and the laws it passes are contrary to the principle of international guarantee.
section_path: THE FACTS
IV. PREPARATORY WORKS

text: The preparatory work on Article 18 of the Convention states that every State which violates human rights and above all the rights of freedom will always have an excuse, such as morality, order, public security and democratic rights.
section_path: THE FACTS
IV. PREPARATORY WORKS

text: The preparatory work on Article 18 of the Convention states that in a democracy, the limitation imposed on individual freedom will be valid only if it has as its aim the public interest and the common good, and that the State may limit an individual freedom in the interests of the freedom of all, in the general interest of a superior freedom of right, in the public interest of the nation.
